projects.title: Persistent Agent: a permanent AI teammate living in your Slack
projects.what: An open source blueprint from LangChain for building an always-on agent in Slack. Put simply, the base for an in-house, proactive team assistant that you adapt to your company.
projects.how: (1) The agent schedules its own work and keeps working toward the goals you give it, without waiting to be asked. (2) It holds playbooks, your organization's best practices and knowledge written down, and enriches them as people use it: this is its memory (it is stateful, it keeps state between conversations). (3) Each person connects their own tools (enterprise connectors such as CRM or Drive). It deploys on LangChain's infrastructure (MDA, according to Harrison Chase).
projects.who: Teams that want agents doing real work in the company. Most agents are reactive (you ask, they answer); this one pursues a goal over time, like an ops analyst you hand a file to. A good starting point to understand how planning, memory and tools fit together.
projects.try: Open source, a template to fork over the weekend according to Harrison Chase. Stars and license not checked. The project link could not be opened (t.co), so details are limited.

projects.title: How Anthropic migrated its API to Rust with a team of agents
projects.what: The story of rewriting Claude's Messages API from Python to Rust, largely by Claude agents, verified against real traffic.
projects.how: Claude wrote a first version in about a week; the real work was proving it behaved the same. (1) Shadowing: each real request goes through the old and the new version and the results are compared step by step. (2) To protect privacy, the text is never read: only a fingerprint of each difference is recorded (which step, which byte, which length). (3) A script groups these differences every 10-30 minutes; a coordinator agent receives each new kind of difference and assigns it to a worker agent, with a Slack thread where engineers follow along and steer. (4) Three loops: an inner loop (sandbox, checks in under a second), an outer loop (validation on production traffic, after human PR review) and a memory loop (human corrections become rules).
projects.who: The key lesson: with AI, generating code gets easy, verifying it becomes the bottleneck. The code passed 98% of its tests but only about 25% of real requests matched at first. Final result: about 70% less CPU per request and about 20% lower latency.
projects.try: Public article, worth reading in full to see a real multi-agent system in production.

projects.title: Agent Lake: LangChain's data lake for agent traces
projects.what: LangSmith's new vision: store every agent trace (the detailed log of each step) and run intelligent compute on top to improve agents. Put simply, a Snowflake specialized for what your agents do.
projects.how: (1) A dedicated database, SmithDB, ingests traces (Clay sends hundreds of millions of events per day). (2) Outcomes are added (the real result: a thumbs down, a merged PR...). (3) Online evals (automatic judges, often an LLM-as-a-judge or a cheaper decision model) label the traces. (4) AI Search lets you search in natural language ("conversations where the user got frustrated"). (5) Agents then analyze these traces to propose fixes.
projects.who: Once an agent runs in production, thousands of traces pile up without telling you whether it is improving. Useful to understand how a business agent is managed over time.
projects.try: Built into LangSmith (paid offering, free trial).

projects.title: Karpathy: a Civilization-style US map built by Claude in 7 hours
projects.what: A vibe-coded side project: Claude (Opus 5.5 in the Claude Code desktop app, ultracode mode) downloaded and combined 31 public data sources (Census, BLS, NOAA, FAA...) to turn them into a game map.
projects.how: All the data is projected onto a grid of 25 km hexagons and translated into game language (gold is GDP, a city's districts are its real industries). 19 lenses, 524 cities, and an Explorer that turns any column for 3,100 counties into a table and scatter plot. 45,000 lines of code in 7 hours.
projects.who: Proof that an agent can do real data-ops work on its own (collecting, cleaning and reconciling heterogeneous sources). Note: it still skipped a few states, and used half of Karpathy's weekly quota.
projects.try: Deployed publicly (link in the tweet), with the source code reachable from the "?" button.

projects.title: Factory becomes free when you bring your own API key
projects.what: Factory (coding agents called Droids) is free for individual developers with BYOK (bring your own key: you pay the model provider directly, not Factory).
projects.how: Download the app, paste your API key, start a task. Temporary bonus: free Droid Computer hours, cloud machines where your agents run in the background (background agents).
projects.who: Worth testing to compare with Claude Code or Codex without another subscription.
projects.try: Free with BYOK, free cloud hours for a limited time. The site could not be opened (factory.ai), so details are limited.
